Cooling energy consumption 15-minute time-series data before and after envelope upgrades 4.2 Stock Energy Impacts 4.2.1 Annual Stock Energy Analysis Figure 5 shows the annual site energy consumption by end use before and after the envelope package upgrades for all homes. The annual stock energy savings from the envelope package upgrade is 938 TWh, compared to a pre-upgrade average consumption of 3,454 TWh— representing a 27.2% reduction. Most savings occured in heating and cooling end uses. This includes 43% (110 TWh) electricity heating savings, 48% (556 TWh) natural gas heating savings, 48% (79 TWh) fuel oil heating savings, 42% (55 TWh) propane heating savings, 72% (16 TWh) electricity heating heat pump backup savings, 24% (91 TWh) electricity cooling savings, 46% (17 TWh) electricity heating fans and pumps savings, and 23% (15 TWh) electricity cooling fans and pumps savings. 10 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Annual site energy consumption for all homes Figure 6 shows the annual energy consumption per dwelling unit by end use before and after the envelope package upgrades for upgraded dwelling units, which includes 98.0% of all dwelling units. The average annual energy savings from the envelope package upgrade is 6,852 kWh, compared to a pre-upgrade average consumption of 24,862 kWh—representing a 27.6% reduction. 11 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 6. Annual site energy consumption per upgraded dwelling unit Table 5 shows the annual energy consumption saving percentage per upgraded dwelling unit. As discussed earlier, most savings were observed in heating and cooling end uses. However, there is only a small change in hot water-related end uses. When both the water heater and ducts are in the same place (e.g., unheated basement, attic), hot water energy consumption can be affected slightly due to reduced heat transfer from the ducts. If the water heater is in the attic, it can be affected by improved attic floor insulation. Additional details are available in the duct sealing and attic floor insulation documentation (Lou & Liu, ResStock 2025 Release 1 SDR Duct Sealing and Insulation Upgrade Documentation, 2025) (Phoung, Lou, & White, 2025b). Furthermore, indoor temperature changes also influence hot water energy use. Overall, the impact on hot water energy consumption is less than 0.1%. There is also a very small change in appliance electricity use, primarily for refrigerators. Refrigerators work by transferring heat from the interior to the surrounding air. When the surrounding air is cooler, a refrigerator operates more efficiently and uses less energy. The average indoor temperature over the year increased slightly from 71.28°F to 71.68°F. This slight increase in temperature results in a minor increase in refrigerator energy use.
